item.title: Dricus Du Plessis sets sights on becoming two-division champ: ‘I’m cutting 45 pounds’
item.description: OKLAHOMA CITY, OKLAHOMA - JULY 18: (R-L) Dricus Du Plessis of South Africa punches Kamaru Usman of Nigeria in a middleweight fight during the UFC Fight Night event at Paycom Center on July 18, 2026 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. (Photo by Jeff Bottari/Zuffa LLC) Dricus Du Plessis is ready for the next chapter of his career, and it involves winning UFC belts in two different weight classes. Du Plessis won the middleweight belt off Sean Strickland back in January 2024 and defended it twice before dropping it to Khamzat Chimaev in a one-sided grappling contest. We’re just over a year removed from that bad loss, and “Stillknocks” has bounced back with a solid win over Kamaru Usman. In a new interview with Sias du Plessis (no relation), Dricus discussed getting back on the winning path. “I think especially after a loss like that, you work so hard to rectify the mistakes that you made,” he said. “And to go back out and go prove that the things you worked on did work, the hard work you put in paid off. It’s incredible. Like I always say, you’re only as good as your last fight, and to be a loser is not in my cards. I don’t like that.” Du Plessis has big ambitions as he works to get himself back into the No. 1 contender spot at 185 pounds. “Getting my belt back,” he stated. “I mean, that’s for me. That’s the biggest thing. I wanna get my belt back, and eventually go up to 205 and go test myself there. And I’m certain that I’ll be a champion. I’m big enough for that division, and I’m certain I can be champion in that division as well.” Du Plessis has always been a big middleweight, and moving up to light heavyweight would take some pressure off his pre-fight cut. “In pounds, it’s 45 pounds that I’m cutting,” he revealed. “Even more sometimes from where I walk around outside of a camp to fight. It’s ridiculous. It’s crazy. But my team is great. We’ve done this for many years. We we got it down to a science. “I’m not gonna sit here and say, ‘No, It’s good for you.’ It isn’t. But, I mean, getting punched in the head is also not good for you. So, I made my choices, and I wouldn’t change it for the world.” Du Plessis says he had some small injuries from the Kamaru Usman fight in July but is ready to go now. He’s definitely at least one solid win away from being back in the top contender’s circle, which isn’t the worst situation given the logjam at the top of 185. As for who, specifically, Dricus wants to fight? “I want to fight the best possible guy because I want to prove that I am the greatest fighter ever,” Du Plessis declared. “And to do that, you can’t just beat a couple of champions. You need to own your route to that title. Take the tough fights that nobody wants, and I’ve been willing to do that.”

item.title: Chad Ryland out-scored the Rams by himself in NFL’s most surprising win of the season
item.description: (Photo by Luke Hales/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Arizona Cardinals and Los Angeles Rams were at opposite ends of our NFL Power Rankings to open the season . The Rams were the obvious No. 1 team in the rankings entering the year after an explosive offseason headed by trades for Myles Garrett and Trent McDuffie. The Cardinals came in at No. 32, dead-last, as they came off a 3-14 season and had major questions at quarterback with Jacoby Brissett slated to be the starter. Six weeks later, the Cardinals and Rams have the exact same record, and it’s the supposedly mighty Rams who find themselves in the cellar of the NFC West after losing to Arizona on Sunday. The Cardinals beat the Rams, 18-16, at SoFi Stadium without scoring a touchdown. Instead, kicker Chad Ryland banged in six field goals, including a 43-yarder to walk it off and win the game. Watch Ryland’s game-winner here: CHAD RYLAND WINS IT FOR THE CARDINALS pic.twitter.com/QfTHlvwVcr — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 The Cardinals consistently sustained long drives against the Rams’ defense, but couldn’t punch the ball in the end zone. That’s where Ryland came in. Here’s a list of his made field goals on the day: 34 yards in the first quarter 30 yards in the second quarter 22 yards in the second quarter 38 yards in the third quarter 27 yards in the fourth quarter 43 yards in the fourth quarter The Cardinals out-played the Rams in every phase of the game. Arizona dominated time of possession at 34:52 to 25:08 for LA. It finished with more yards (338 to 286) by out-gaining the Rams through the air and the ground. The Cardinals had more first downs, too. A couple years ago, Ryland missed a kick for the New England Patriots that landed them the pick that became Drake Maye. He’ll be a New England icon forever for that one even if he’s a career 77% kicker during his time in the league. Ryland now has another fan base that should love him, if only because the Cardinals beating the Rams should have been absolutely impossible based on preseason expectations. And that’s why they play the games.

item.title: 49ers-Commanders: Brock Purdy primed for a huge day? How many losses for S.F. this season?
item.description: After tangling with Seattle's rugged defense last week, quarterback Brock Purdy should find the going easier when the 49ers face the Commanders on Monday. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) The San Francisco 49ers , however battered and bruised they might be, are 5-0 and the toast of the NFL in the early going. The Washington Commanders roll into Levi's Stadium for Monday Night Football in the wake of an embarrassing tie against the New York Giants. As the Niners bid to keep their record perfect, we asked columnist Ann Killion and reporters Eric Branch and Harrison Rich for their thoughts about the big questions before this game - and a prediction of the outcome. Nobody expected 5-0, but now Nate Silver puts the 49ers' playoff chances at 97% and their chance to win the division at almost 80%. Is that believable? How many losses do you think the 49ers wind up with this season? Ann Killion: It's an amazing sprint out of the gate, one that not many people saw coming. Not with the stress of Australia, facing their top two division foes in the first five games, and a date with one of last season's AFC contenders. The 49ers weathered this first third of the schedule and the middle third is pretty forgiving. It's that last third that might be gnarly, when injuries might mount, there are a lot of road games, and the reality that the 49ers have recently had more trouble with the Rams and Seahawks at Levi's than on the road. I think they'll end up with four or five losses. I'm not a Nate Silver fan but, yeah, you don't need to be a poker-playing statistician to predict they make the playoffs and possibly win the division. Harrison Rich: We're about to be a third of the way through the regular season, and if the Niners can handle business Monday night against the Commanders - which they should, considering they're 7.5-point favorites - it'll mark their first 6-0 start since 2019. Remind me how far they made it that season? Oh, right, the Super Bowl. I'm not saying they're a lock to play on Valentine's Day, but it's looking like the 49ers could be 9-0 a month from now. If that happens, winning the division would essentially be a lock, as would a playoff berth. And a three- or four-loss season would certainly be on the table. Eric Branch: Watch out, 1972 Dolphins. OK, that's a joke, but it won't be a surprise if Larry Csonka and his old teammates are waiting on the 49ers to finally lose this season so they can pop the Champagne to celebrate remaining the NFL's only unbeaten team. The 49ers' upcoming slate: Commanders, Falcons, Raiders, Cowboys. Yes, 9-0 is possible and at least 8-1 almost seems assured. Of course, the NFL is wildly unpredictable and injuries are always a massive factor. If the 49ers can remain reasonably healthy - so far, Brock Purdy , Christian McCaffrey , Mike Evans , George Kittle , Trent Williams and Fred Warner haven't missed a game - is 13-4 their floor? item.content:encoded: After tangling with Seattle's rugged defense last week, quarterback Brock Purdy should find the going easier when the 49ers face the Commanders on Monday. (Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle) The San Francisco 49ers , however battered and bruised they might be, are 5-0 and the toast of the NFL in the early going. The Washington Commanders roll into Levi's Stadium for Monday Night Football in the wake of an embarrassing tie against the New York Giants. As the Niners bid to keep their record perfect, we asked columnist Ann Killion and reporters Eric Branch and Harrison Rich for their thoughts about the big questions before this game - and a prediction of the outcome. Nobody expected 5-0, but now Nate Silver puts the 49ers' playoff chances at 97% and their chance to win the division at almost 80%. Is that believable? How many losses do you think the 49ers wind up with this season? Ann Killion: It's an amazing sprint out of the gate, one that not many people saw coming. Not with the stress of Australia, facing their top two division foes in the first five games, and a date with one of last season's AFC contenders. The 49ers weathered this first third of the schedule and the middle third is pretty forgiving. It's that last third that might be gnarly, when injuries might mount, there are a lot of road games, and the reality that the 49ers have recently had more trouble with the Rams and Seahawks at Levi's than on the road. I think they'll end up with four or five losses. I'm not a Nate Silver fan but, yeah, you don't need to be a poker-playing statistician to predict they make the playoffs and possibly win the division. Harrison Rich: We're about to be a third of the way through the regular season, and if the Niners can handle business Monday night against the Commanders - which they should, considering they're 7.5-point favorites - it'll mark their first 6-0 start since 2019. Remind me how far they made it that season? Oh, right, the Super Bowl. I'm not saying they're a lock to play on Valentine's Day, but it's looking like the 49ers could be 9-0 a month from now. If that happens, winning the division would essentially be a lock, as would a playoff berth. And a three- or four-loss season would certainly be on the table. Eric Branch: Watch out, 1972 Dolphins. OK, that's a joke, but it won't be a surprise if Larry Csonka and his old teammates are waiting on the 49ers to finally lose this season so they can pop the Champagne to celebrate remaining the NFL's only unbeaten team. The 49ers' upcoming slate: Commanders, Falcons, Raiders, Cowboys. Yes, 9-0 is possible and at least 8-1 almost seems assured. Of course, the NFL is wildly unpredictable and injuries are always a massive factor. If the 49ers can remain reasonably healthy - so far, Brock Purdy , Christian McCaffrey , Mike Evans , George Kittle , Trent Williams and Fred Warner haven't missed a game - is 13-4 their floor? How much will Dre Greenlaw 's absence hurt this defense, or did the win over the Seahawks put those kinds of concerns to rest? Killion: I think Greenlaw's absence will be felt, especially when facing a mobile quarterback. He is an emotional leader for the team and he and Warner have made some beautiful music together this season. The 49ers might also be missing the spark of Deebo Samuel on the other side of the ball; like Greenlaw felt against Denver, Samuel was surely looking forward to playing against the team he was with last year, when the consensus was that he was "washed." Both Greenlaw and Samuel have been key sparks in this 5-0 run. Rich: A void will be felt in the middle of the 49ers' defense without their emotional leader. But with the way defensive coordinator Raheem Morris has his unit playing, I'm not sure any one-week absence (outside of Warner) is truly debilitating. San Francisco should survive the Commanders without him. As a bonus, I'm looking forward to watching rookie linebacker Jaden Dugger with an increased role. He impressed in spurts against Seattle, collecting a sack off the edge before filling in admirably as an off-ball linebacker after Greenlaw exited. Branch: The 49ers held up OK without Greenlaw against Seattle, but the Seahawks' offense is a mess. The Commanders aren't exactly "The Greatest Show on Turf," but Greenlaw's absence could be felt when it comes to tracking down elusive QB Jayden Daniels. It will be interesting to see if Dugger can limit the dropoff. When it comes to Greenlaw's impact, I'll always think back to his 2024 debut in Week 15 in a 12-6 loss to the Rams. For two quarters, it was remarkable to see how his energy and ability elevated what had been an ordinary defense. The Commanders have been giving up close to 30 points per game. Do you think this makes for a big game for Brock Purdy and Co.? Killion: Purdy is playing at a different level this year, quicker decision-making, more authoritative. So, sure, he might hang 30-plus on the Commanders. But if he doesn't have Evans, who missed a lot of practice, and Samuel, who is out, it might be tougher than it seems on paper. But, sure, after beating Denver's and Seattle's defense in back-to-back weeks, the 49ers' offense could feast on Monday. Rich: No offense to Giants quarterback Jameis Winston, but if he can throw for three touchdowns with no interceptions while collecting a 96.7 passer rating against the Commanders, Purdy should be able to move the ball downfield with his eyes closed. Washington's secondary is swiss cheese. Purdy struggled plenty last week against the Seahawks, but Seattle is his kryptonite. Expect the 49ers' quarterback to beat up on another low-level defense, similar to how he shredded the Dolphins and Cardinals a few weeks back. Branch: Purdy is approaching that level where every week, regardless of the opponent's defense, could be yet another game with multiple touchdown passes and a 115-plus QB rating. That said, last week's big win in Seattle largely obscured the fact that Purdy led an offense that had 133 yards and six first downs in the first 42 minutes against a suffocating defense. Purdy and his teammates will have far more room to breathe against the NFL's 23rd-ranked defense. And now, everyone's least favorite part: Will the 49ers still be undefeated on Tuesday morning, or do the Commanders pull off an upset? Killion: Is my picking against the 49ers the secret to their success? Maybe. I'm willing to test out the reverse theory this week. The Commanders are in desperation mode after last week's disastrous ending, one of the most embarrassing things I've witnessed in a lifetime of watching this league. But I still don't think Washington is going to be able to muster enough to beat one of the best teams in the league. 49ers 31, Commanders 20. Rich: You won't catch me trying to predict the Niners' first loss this week. The Commanders' offense could make things interesting with Daniels, but I don't expect their defense to hold up over 60 minutes. 49ers 34, Commanders 17 Branch: After picking against the 49ers for three straight weeks (0-3, obviously), I'll provide the kiss of death by picking them to win. The Commanders do have Daniels and it will be interesting to see how the 49ers defense handles a QB who will easily be the most mobile they've faced this season. But the chances of Daniels - and his team - summoning that 2024 magic appears unlikely: They are 6-15-1 since reaching the NFC Championship Game. 49ers 34, Commanders 21 Subscribe There’s more to San Francisco with the Chronicle. Subscribe today for just 25¢. This article originally published at 49ers-Commanders: Brock Purdy primed for a huge day? How many losses for S.F. this season? .

item.title: 3 things we learned from Michigan Football’s win over Penn State
item.description: ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 17: Tommy Carr #14 of the Michigan Wolverines celebrates after a play during the second half of a college football game against the Penn State Nittany Lions at Michigan Stadium on October 17, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The Michigan Wolverines won the game 21-18. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The bye week and a troublesome offensie performance in the first half led to a quarterback change for Michigan on Saturday, leading to a 21-18 win in the Big House. True freshman Tommy Carr stepped in and led the Wolverines to three second-half scoring drives and the eventual victory. Newfound optimism courses through the veins of Schembechler Hall, but there’s still much to prove and a lot to take away from this performance. Let’s dig into what could be the turning point of the season. Bryce Underwood and Jason Beck cannot operate together The switch under center has felt like a long time coming, and the fact of the matter is Underwood and Beck operate on two different wavelengths. Beck’s scheme and system don’t match Underwood’s strengths, and Underwood could not operate what Beck wanted to do with his offense. A first half with 154 yards of total offense, as well as two interceptions from the former five-star, meant a change was inevitable. Underwood’s final six quarters as the starter equated to 15-of-32 passing for 144 yards, four interceptions and zero touchdowns. After the loss to Minnesota, I said in this series Michigan failed Underwood. I still believe that to be true. It’s not like Underwood isn’t the athletic specimen that shot him up recruiting boards and made him one of the most highly sought after players in college football history. He’s routinely displayed arm talent and capabilities that 99.9 percent of humans cannot replicate. But under his second system in as many years, where the coaching staff has asked him to make multiple reads against Big Ten-caliber defenses, Underwood hasn’t been able to execute to the level he needed to in order to keep his job. And he attempted to adjust his skillset and become more of the rushing quarterback Beck wanted, to limited success. The nail is now in the coffin. There is no world where Beck and Underwood can coexist. Beck’s scheme doesn’t allow for Michigan to spread the ball out, take deep shots and get Underwood out of the pocket consistently to make easy reads. It’s a complex system that requires quick decisions in the right place, multiple reads and a quarterback mobile enough to keep it themselves. item.content:encoded: ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 17: Tommy Carr #14 of the Michigan Wolverines celebrates after a play during the second half of a college football game against the Penn State Nittany Lions at Michigan Stadium on October 17, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The Michigan Wolverines won the game 21-18. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The bye week and a troublesome offensie performance in the first half led to a quarterback change for Michigan on Saturday, leading to a 21-18 win in the Big House. True freshman Tommy Carr stepped in and led the Wolverines to three second-half scoring drives and the eventual victory. Newfound optimism courses through the veins of Schembechler Hall, but there’s still much to prove and a lot to take away from this performance. Let’s dig into what could be the turning point of the season. Bryce Underwood and Jason Beck cannot operate together The switch under center has felt like a long time coming, and the fact of the matter is Underwood and Beck operate on two different wavelengths. Beck’s scheme and system don’t match Underwood’s strengths, and Underwood could not operate what Beck wanted to do with his offense. A first half with 154 yards of total offense, as well as two interceptions from the former five-star, meant a change was inevitable. Underwood’s final six quarters as the starter equated to 15-of-32 passing for 144 yards, four interceptions and zero touchdowns. After the loss to Minnesota, I said in this series Michigan failed Underwood. I still believe that to be true. It’s not like Underwood isn’t the athletic specimen that shot him up recruiting boards and made him one of the most highly sought after players in college football history. He’s routinely displayed arm talent and capabilities that 99.9 percent of humans cannot replicate. But under his second system in as many years, where the coaching staff has asked him to make multiple reads against Big Ten-caliber defenses, Underwood hasn’t been able to execute to the level he needed to in order to keep his job. And he attempted to adjust his skillset and become more of the rushing quarterback Beck wanted, to limited success. The nail is now in the coffin. There is no world where Beck and Underwood can coexist. Beck’s scheme doesn’t allow for Michigan to spread the ball out, take deep shots and get Underwood out of the pocket consistently to make easy reads. It’s a complex system that requires quick decisions in the right place, multiple reads and a quarterback mobile enough to keep it themselves. Whittingham decided in the bye week to trust his offensive coordinator over his quarterback. On Saturday, it appeared to be the right call. But the video game quarterback that is Bryce Underwood will very likely find another program in the offseason, and it would not be a surprise if he can find success if it is one that allows him to develop and focus on where he is naturally gifted instead of forcing him into something he isn’t. Tommy Carr is capable of leading this offense In just a half of football, the difference Carr made on the field was obvious. From the spark that many saw in the spring game to Saturday, it’s clear Carr has quickly picked up what Beck wants this Michigan offense to look like. What I saw was a quarterback getting the ball out of his hands quickly, consistently making the right reads and being on the same page as everyone else. He didn’t try to go in and be Superman, Carr simply stepped in and executed. Nothing he did was particularly flashy or outstanding, but he operated at a level this offense has not seen in 2026. That allowed the playbook to open up, because really what a lot of Michigan’s RPO-style offense affords is a triple option. Defenses often have to determine whether Carr is going to hand it off, keep it himself or make a quick throw to a receiver either over the middle or on the boundary. The difference with the ball in the hands of Carr compared to Underwood in this role was apparent, as the Wolverines scored all 21 of their points in the second half and finished with more than 300 total yards. If (and this is a big if) Carr can continue at this pace, there is plenty of reason for excitement as we head down the stretch of the 2026 campaign. Michigan’s defense (not Carr) won them this game Carr was great, but let’s take off our maize and blue glasses for a second here and just evaluate what really happened in the second half. Each of Michigan’s second-half touchdowns came off a turnover, and the Wolverines took over on a short field twice. Advantageous opportunities were abundant for Carr in his first legitimate playing time of the season. What I implore Michigan fans to do is to not put Carr on a pedestal. It’s way too early to call Carr the savior of this program or even this season. He did a nice job taking care of business in the opportunity that was laid in front of him, but the defense is really what set him up for success. My fear here has two prongs. First, is that the pressure of being the quarterback of a blue blood program like Michigan as a true freshman. There are going to be things said about Carr this week that can easily pivot focus and mentality. All the while, preparation is likely going to be different for him this week, as it appears he will make his first start. Pinning this second half as more than his stat lline — 5-of-7 for 83 total yards and a touchdown — is more harm than good. The reason for that is my second point — who Michigan’s next game is against. The Indiana Hoosiers are out for blood after losing a game they shouldn’t have to Ohio State. Curt Cignetti and the Hoosiers are not in the same stratosphere as Matt Campbell and his defense that is allowing 398 yards per game to Big Ten opponents. Carr is getting thrown into the deep end against one of the best coaches, defenses and programs in college football today. Rewind about 400 days ago, and wasn’t that the exact same scenario Underwood was at playing in Norman against Oklahoma? And didn’t the hoopla of calling for his head start pretty quickly after that? My biggest fear is this being a mistake for not allowing Carr the opportunity to sit and learn for longer, forcing something that looked promising into something much shorter lived. The mindset here for Michigan fans should be, at best, cautiously optimistic. Anything more than that, especially dialogue about a quarterback change solving all their problems, is farfetched with only one half of football as evidence and a true freshman leading the way.

item.title: What's causing Texas QB Arch Manning's late turnover woes? We watched the film.
item.description: Texas quarterback Arch Manning (16) is tackled during the game against Florida at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 in Austin. (Aaron E. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman) Arch Manning committed a turnover on Texas football 's final drive in each of its last two losses. Both turnovers featured one commonality: a blitzing player from the opposing defense. The pair of turnovers have played as a saddening slideshow for Longhorns fans across the last 10 days. Texas (4-2, 1-2 SEC) limped out of the Cotton Bowl in Dallas after a 27-24 loss on Oct. 10, where the fourth quarter featured a pick-six from Manning, a subsequent touchdown drive and then another interception before Oklahoma's walk-off field goal. MORE: How did Texas grade out in its loss to Florida? Not too good. MORE: Just exactly who is KJ Lacey, Arch Manning's backup QB at Texas? Manning had a chance at redemption Saturday with Texas trailing Florida 27-24 in the game's final minutes. Manning and Texas' offense received the ball at Royal-Memorial Stadium with 2 minutes, 27 seconds remaining. They gave the ball back to Florida two plays later, the result of a sack of Manning and subsequent fumble recovery by the Gators. ARCH MANNING THROWS A COSTLY INTERCEPTION WITH 20 SECONDS LEFT!! https://t.co/Hq9o38IUzf - ESPN (@espn) October 10, 2026 The cause of the turnovers may not be entirely apparent at first glance. Let's take a deeper look at the film of each backbreaking turnover, with commentary from both Manning and head coach Steve Sarkisian . Dropped eyes, missed man Check the alignment here before the snap on Texas' final offensive play. Circled is Florida senior Kanye Clark, identified by Manning after the game as the "star" linebacker. The star acts as an extra defensive back, one that can drop into coverage or rush the passer. Florida defensive back Kanye Clark lined up as the "star" blitzer on Arch Manning's game-sealing interception on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 (via X) Clark chose to rush the passer from the right side, and Florida linebacker Myles Graham provided additional pressure up the middle. But such pressure shouldn't necessarily wreck a play, especially when the proper outlet is provided. Manning had exactly that on the critical sack and subsequent fumble. Manning's had wide receiver Emmett Mosley V open on an out route early in the play, seen circled cutting toward the right sideline after running just past the 50-yard line. Texas quarterback Arch Manning missed open wide receiver Emmett Mosley V before his crucial sack and subsequent fumble in a loss to Florida on Oct. 17, 2026 (via X) Manning didn't pull the trigger and throw to Mosley. He instead looked toward the middle of the field, received oncoming pressure, and was sacked. He was flung into Texas left tackle Trevor Goosby on the play, and the collision jarred the ball loose for a Florida recovery. Not sure why Arch doesn't throw the Out route to Mosley? He's literally staring right at Mo
item.content:encoded: Texas quarterback Arch Manning (16) is tackled during the game against Florida at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 in Austin. (Aaron E. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman) Arch Manning committed a turnover on Texas football 's final drive in each of its last two losses. Both turnovers featured one commonality: a blitzing player from the opposing defense. The pair of turnovers have played as a saddening slideshow for Longhorns fans across the last 10 days. Texas (4-2, 1-2 SEC) limped out of the Cotton Bowl in Dallas after a 27-24 loss on Oct. 10, where the fourth quarter featured a pick-six from Manning, a subsequent touchdown drive and then another interception before Oklahoma's walk-off field goal. MORE: How did Texas grade out in its loss to Florida? Not too good. MORE: Just exactly who is KJ Lacey, Arch Manning's backup QB at Texas? Manning had a chance at redemption Saturday with Texas trailing Florida 27-24 in the game's final minutes. Manning and Texas' offense received the ball at Royal-Memorial Stadium with 2 minutes, 27 seconds remaining. They gave the ball back to Florida two plays later, the result of a sack of Manning and subsequent fumble recovery by the Gators. ARCH MANNING THROWS A COSTLY INTERCEPTION WITH 20 SECONDS LEFT!! https://t.co/Hq9o38IUzf - ESPN (@espn) October 10, 2026 The cause of the turnovers may not be entirely apparent at first glance. Let's take a deeper look at the film of each backbreaking turnover, with commentary from both Manning and head coach Steve Sarkisian . Dropped eyes, missed man Check the alignment here before the snap on Texas' final offensive play. Circled is Florida senior Kanye Clark, identified by Manning after the game as the "star" linebacker. The star acts as an extra defensive back, one that can drop into coverage or rush the passer. Florida defensive back Kanye Clark lined up as the "star" blitzer on Arch Manning's game-sealing interception on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 (via X) Clark chose to rush the passer from the right side, and Florida linebacker Myles Graham provided additional pressure up the middle. But such pressure shouldn't necessarily wreck a play, especially when the proper outlet is provided. Manning had exactly that on the critical sack and subsequent fumble. Manning's had wide receiver Emmett Mosley V open on an out route early in the play, seen circled cutting toward the right sideline after running just past the 50-yard line. Texas quarterback Arch Manning missed open wide receiver Emmett Mosley V before his crucial sack and subsequent fumble in a loss to Florida on Oct. 17, 2026 (via X) Manning didn't pull the trigger and throw to Mosley. He instead looked toward the middle of the field, received oncoming pressure, and was sacked. He was flung into Texas left tackle Trevor Goosby on the play, and the collision jarred the ball loose for a Florida recovery. Not sure why Arch doesn't throw the Out route to Mosley? He's literally staring right at Mosley. Arch sees Nickel blitz so you have a perfect call to what Florida is sending but he just doesn't throw the football https://t.co/g3ArAWwnNb - LandonTengwall (@LandonTengwall) October 18, 2026 Texas' quarterback said he "lost" Mosley running toward the sideline, resulting in a sack. Sarkisian gave a more detailed explanation. "I think (Manning) might have been a little quick to drop his eyes," Sarkisian said. "He had Emmett Mosley, who was the primary, he could have got the ball out, but then ultimately the protection broke down." Texas running back Hollywood Smothers (2) runs the ball during the game against Florida at Darrell K Royal–Texas Memorial Stadium on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026 in Austin. (Aaron E. Martinez/Austin American-Statesman) Game of inches for Texas Manning made a mental error in the game-ending turnover vs. Florida. His process on the final drive against Oklahoma was more sound. Oklahoma sent what Manning called last week a "boundary sting (blitz)," on the deciding play of this year's Red River Rivalry. The blitzer in question here is Oklahoma defensive back Michael Boganowski, circled below. Arch Manning was blitzed by Oklahoma before his second interception of the afternoon in Texas' 27-24 loss in Dallas on Oct. 10, 2026 (via X) Boganowski breaks through Texas' offensive line untouched on the play, and Manning receives additional pressure from edge rusher Danny Okoye. Manning is crunched on the throw by multiple defenders. He still made the correct read in a crowded situation, targeting 6-foot-3 wide receiver Cam Coleman on a 1-on-1 comeback route on the right sideline. Arch Manning faced pressure from Oklahoma's defensive line before his second interception of Texas' 27-24 loss in Dallas on Oct. 10, 2026 (via X) Throw the ball farther toward the sideline, and Texas should either register a 12-yard completion or suffer a harmless incompletion on second-and-10. Manning instead keeps the throw closer toward midfield, and right into the arms of Oklahoma defensive back Courtland Guillory. "They brought a boundary sting (blitz). I had to get it out," Manning said last week. "I have to get it more outside to Cam or get an incompletion to stop the clock and get another down. Obviously you can't do that in that situation." ARCH MANNING THROWS A COSTLY INTERCEPTION WITH 20 SECONDS LEFT!! https://t.co/Hq9o38IUzf - ESPN (@espn) October 10, 2026 Two one-score losses, two game-sealing turnovers. The errors are in part what's caused Texas to lose back-to-back games, a stunning eight-day stretch that tumbled the nation's No. 1 team to No. 19 in the Associated Press top 25. Manning's immense skill still flashes. So does his immaturity and inconsistency. One missed throw and one botched read led to two of Manning's career low-lights in Austin, calling into question his starting spot just seven games into his highly hyped senior season. item.title: Who will back up Yainer Diaz at catcher? | Houston Astros roster analysis
item.description: Houston Astros Yainer Diaz (21) reacts after striking out to end the fourth inning during Game 1 of an American League Wild Card Series in Houston, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle) Sixth in a series on the Houston Astros ' 2026 season, which ended with an AL West title but a sweep in the opening round of the playoffs. Catcher For their catching tandem in 2026, the Houston Astros paired primary receiver Yainer Diaz's offense-first profile with a seasoned backup in Christian Vázquez . An oblique injury that cost Diaz six weeks resulted in Vázquez making just two fewer starts than Diaz behind the plate. The overall result resembled a counterbalancing of their traits. Houston's catchers ranked 17th out of 30 major-league teams in OPS, buoyed by Diaz's second-half upturn. They totaled minus-1 defensive runs saved, per Sports Info Solutions, with Vázquez's positive marks neutralized by Diaz's numbers. Diaz and Vázquez combined to start all but 10 games at catcher for the Astros, with César Salazar and Collin Price covering the balance. They combined to accrue 1.6 wins above replacement, per Baseball Reference, which ranked 19th, while FanGraphs assessed them 1.7 WAR, which ranked 21st. What went right Offensively, Diaz rebounded from a slow start. Diaz batted .248 with a .688 OPS before the All-Star break, then hit .318 with an .850 OPS after the break and a .364/.394/.626 slash line in his final 28 games. Diaz had a career-high 54.7% groundball rate and a career-low 38.8% hard-hit rate and continued to chase out of the zone at a garish 42.1% clip. But among catchers with at least 200 plate appearances, he ranked fourth in batting average (.282), seventh in slugging (.475) and 11th in weighted runs created-plus (116). Defensively, Vázquez compiled a strong season by public metrics. Sports Info Solutions assessed him six defensive runs saved; just 11 players who logged an inning at catcher accrued more. Statcast gave him a plus-5 fielding run value, 12th among its 45 qualified catchers. Vázquez was worth plus-six runs via pitch framing, per Baseball Savant, tied for fifth-most at the position. He also rated 1.8 runs above average at ABS challenges, per Statcast, which ranked eighth among catchers. Houston Astros catcher Yainer Diaz, right, gets between Taylor Trammell and umpire Ryan Additon after Trammell was called out on strikes to end the top of the second inning of an MLB baseball game at Sutter Health Park in Sacramento, California, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle) What went wrong Defensively, Diaz rated poorly in public metrics. Sports Info Solutions assessed him minus-7 runs saved, tied for the fourth-worst mark at catcher, while Statcast assessed him a minus-5 fielding run value, tied for sixth-lowest. Diaz accrued minus-4 runs from pitch framing, per Statcast, with neutral performances in blocking and throwing. He did throw out 23% of would-be base-stealers, matching the MLB average. He rate
item.content:encoded: Houston Astros Yainer Diaz (21) reacts after striking out to end the fourth inning during Game 1 of an American League Wild Card Series in Houston, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026. (Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle) Sixth in a series on the Houston Astros ' 2026 season, which ended with an AL West title but a sweep in the opening round of the playoffs. Catcher For their catching tandem in 2026, the Houston Astros paired primary receiver Yainer Diaz's offense-first profile with a seasoned backup in Christian Vázquez . An oblique injury that cost Diaz six weeks resulted in Vázquez making just two fewer starts than Diaz behind the plate. The overall result resembled a counterbalancing of their traits. Houston's catchers ranked 17th out of 30 major-league teams in OPS, buoyed by Diaz's second-half upturn. They totaled minus-1 defensive runs saved, per Sports Info Solutions, with Vázquez's positive marks neutralized by Diaz's numbers. Diaz and Vázquez combined to start all but 10 games at catcher for the Astros, with César Salazar and Collin Price covering the balance. They combined to accrue 1.6 wins above replacement, per Baseball Reference, which ranked 19th, while FanGraphs assessed them 1.7 WAR, which ranked 21st. What went right Offensively, Diaz rebounded from a slow start. Diaz batted .248 with a .688 OPS before the All-Star break, then hit .318 with an .850 OPS after the break and a .364/.394/.626 slash line in his final 28 games. Diaz had a career-high 54.7% groundball rate and a career-low 38.8% hard-hit rate and continued to chase out of the zone at a garish 42.1% clip. But among catchers with at least 200 plate appearances, he ranked fourth in batting average (.282), seventh in slugging (.475) and 11th in weighted runs created-plus (116). Defensively, Vázquez compiled a strong season by public metrics. Sports Info Solutions assessed him six defensive runs saved; just 11 players who logged an inning at catcher accrued more. Statcast gave him a plus-5 fielding run value, 12th among its 45 qualified catchers. Vázquez was worth plus-six runs via pitch framing, per Baseball Savant, tied for fifth-most at the position. He also rated 1.8 runs above average at ABS challenges, per Statcast, which ranked eighth among catchers. Houston Astros catcher Yainer Diaz, right, gets between Taylor Trammell and umpire Ryan Additon after Trammell was called out on strikes to end the top of the second inning of an MLB baseball game at Sutter Health Park in Sacramento, California, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (Jason Fochtman/Houston Chronicle) What went wrong Defensively, Diaz rated poorly in public metrics. Sports Info Solutions assessed him minus-7 runs saved, tied for the fourth-worst mark at catcher, while Statcast assessed him a minus-5 fielding run value, tied for sixth-lowest. Diaz accrued minus-4 runs from pitch framing, per Statcast, with neutral performances in blocking and throwing. He did throw out 23% of would-be base-stealers, matching the MLB average. He rated minus-0.6 runs above average for ABS challenges, per Statcast, despite a 57% overturn rate. It marked a step back for Diaz in his third season as the primary catcher. Framing pitches at the bottom of the strike zone remained a weakness (minus-5 runs saved, per Statcast). Vázquez's framing resulted in an overall positive mark from Astros catchers, but they had net negative marks in blocking (minus-2) and throwing (minus-1). If factoring in pitchers' performance, the Astros allowed the seventh-most runs per game, with the majors' 12th-highest strikeout rate (22.8%) and second-highest walk rate (10.5%). Number to note 25%: Caught stealing percentage for Houston. Teams ran nearly at will against the Astros in 2025, when they ranked 29th in caught-stealing percentage (16%) and stolen bases allowed (157) despite making combatting the running game a point of emphasis. This season brought progress, albeit modest. That involved both the pitchers and catchers. Baseball Savant's "estimated caught stealing" metric for catchers calculates the probability of throwing out a runner based on factors including the runner's speed, where he is when the pitch is received and pitch location. In 2025, Astros catchers had a 17% estimated caught stealing rate, tied for lowest in the majors, indicating their pitchers were not giving them chances to throw out runners. This season, it was 23%. Just five teams had a higher one. The catchers, meanwhile, logged an actual 22% caught stealing rate, per Baseball Savant. Though lower than their estimated caught stealing rate, it was up from 15% last season, indicating the catchers did a better job of converting their throw opportunities. Vázquez had an actual caught stealing rate of 25%, compared to an expected 22% rate, and Diaz had an 18% actual rate compared to a 17% expected rate. Contract status Diaz is entering his second year of salary arbitration eligibility. Last offseason, Diaz and the Astros failed to reach a salary agreement by the deadline to exchange figures and went to an arbitration hearing. Diaz won the hearing and received a $4.5 million salary; the Astros had submitted at $3 million. MLB Trade Rumors projects Diaz will receive a raise to $6.3 million for 2027. Vázquez, whom the Astros initially signed to a minor-league deal this spring, is set to reach free agency again. After concluding a three-year, $30 million deal with the Twins, during which he played 260 games and accrued 0.1 bWAR, Vázquez went unsigned last offseason until mid-March. But he could generate interest as a veteran backup this winter after filling that role suitably with Houston. Jason Schiavone (55) could take a jump to majors next season. Cather poses with Will Bush (56) at spring training last March. (Kelly Gavin/MLB Photos via Getty Images) In the minors The biggest breakout in Houston's minor-league system this year belonged to catcher Jason Schiavone. An 11th-round draft pick playing his second full professional season, Schiavone became the first minor-league catcher since 1981 to record a 30-home run, 30-steal campaign. He climbed two levels to finish the season at Triple-A and the Astros named him their minor-league player of the year. Schiavone compiled a .922 OPS across 123 games this season, starting 69 of them at catcher along with 29 at first base and 24 at designated hitter. He exhibited some swing-and-miss tendency – a 65.1% contact rate, per FanGraphs, and a 32% strikeout rate – while also drawing a 17.4% walk rate. He will play winter ball in the Dominican Republic to continue his development this offseason. Walker Janek, the Astros' 2024 first-round pick and a non-roster invitee to major-league spring training this year, played in 72 games during the season due to injuries. Janek spent most of that at Double-A, where he hit .230 with a .643 OPS in 59 games. Janek fell to No. 21 in MLB Pipeline's latest ratings of the Astros' prospects and No. 27 on Baseball America's list. Houston Astros catcher Christian Vazquez flips his bat after slapping a 2-run single off Los Angeles Angels starting pitcher Jack Kochanowicz during the second inning of a Major League Baseball game at Daikin Park in Houston, Sunday, March 29, 2026. (Brett Coomer/Houston Chronicle) Key question Do the Astros see Schiavone contributing at the major-league level in 2027? Schiavone began this season at High-A and played just nine games at Triple-A before it ended. But his abrupt ascent invites the question of whether the Astros envision him being a factor in 2027. If so, it could impact their approach to the catching position this offseason. At the least, with Vázquez poised to be a free agent, the Astros will need to fill the backup role, whether by retaining Vázquez, making an outside addition or promoting from within. They did not entrust Salazar with that role this spring. Price, who is on the 40-man roster, appeared in just seven games in a brief call-up. Houston's recent stance has been th

item.title: WNBA Finals Game 2 discussion: Can the Atlanta Dream prove they have what it takes to beat the Golden State Valkyries?
item.description: The Atlanta Dream starting five. | Getty Images The Golden State Valkyries know who they are. The pillars of their identity—defense and depth, plus the the clutchtime magic of Ballhalla—were the foundation of their Game 1 win in the 2026 WNBA Finals over the Atlanta Dream. Through their 5-0 start to the postseason, the Dream had appeared to discover their identity, flexing an aggression and athleticism that overwhelmed the Washington Mystics and New York Liberty. But, what if they can’t access that very best version of themselves? If the defensive aggression does not lead to a torrent of turnovers that produces tons of transition offense, then what happens? If the opponent can match their athleticism, neutralizing advantages earned through speed, length and energy, what’s the alternative? Those are the questions facing the Dream as they prepare for Game 2 of the WNBA Finals. Can Atlanta reassert who they are against a Golden State team that seems perfectly suited to snuff out the Dream’s strengths, evidenced by the Valkyries’ now 4-0 record against the Dream across the 2026 regular season and playoffs? Alternatively, can the Dream find an expanded version of themselves, solving the problems the Valkyries have presented through tweaked tactics and shifted strategies? After Game 1, the Dream expressed an intent to rediscover their identity. Speaking to Atlanta News First’s Baillie Burmaster, Rhyne Howard asserted that the Dream “didn’t punch back” and instead “played to how they were making us play,” noting that Atlanta must “play like we’ve been playing the regular postseason” and not “let them dictate how we want to play.” POSTGAME: Caught up with Rhyne Howard following the Dream's game one loss to the Valkyries in the WNBA Finals @ATLNewsFirst #WNBAFinals pic.twitter.com/dtkeedJ3cP — Baillie Burmaster (@baillie_burm) October 17, 2026 In the postgame press conference, Angel Reese was similarly insistent, suggesting her scoreless second half was not the product of defensive adjustments from Golden State but about her own lack of necessary aggression. Angel Reese on not taking a lot of shot attempts in the 2nd half: "I wasn't aggressive enough with the ball…definitely gonna do a better job of that next game" pic.twitter.com/3ikrLV5MyO — Oh No He Didn't 🤯 (@ohnohedidnt24) October 17, 2026 There’s reason to believe that the Dream are right. Heading into Game 1, they not only were undefeated in the playoffs but also had won a franchise-record 10-straight games. Such a streak of success suggests that one loss should not inspire significant change. As head coach Karl Smesko said, “We were right there. Right there. That’s why it hurts a little bit, but it also motivates us.” Dream presser was a lot of shorter answers from players. Atlanta felt it could win that game. Appeared upset with result. Karl Smesko: “We’re gonna look at everything we're gonna watch and try to get better, but, I mean, we were right there, right there.⁰⁰“So that's why it… — Meghan
item.content:encoded: The Atlanta Dream starting five. | Getty Images The Golden State Valkyries know who they are. The pillars of their identity—defense and depth, plus the the clutchtime magic of Ballhalla—were the foundation of their Game 1 win in the 2026 WNBA Finals over the Atlanta Dream. Angel Reese on not taking a lot of shot attempts in the 2nd half: "I wasn't aggressive enough with the ball…definitely gonna do a better job of that next game" pic.twitter.com/3ikrLV5MyO — Oh No He Didn't 🤯 (@ohnohedidnt24) October 17, 2026 There’s reason to believe that the Dream are right. Heading into Game 1, they not only were undefeated in the playoffs but also had won a franchise-record 10-straight games. That’s why it hurts a little bit, but it also motivates us.” Dream presser was a lot of shorter answers from players. Atlanta felt it could win that game. Appeared upset with result. Karl Smesko: “We’re gonna look at everything we're gonna watch and try to get better, but, I mean, we were right there, right there.⁰⁰“So that's why it… — Meghan L. Hall (@ItsMeghanLHall) October 17, 2026 Game 1 also offered more than enough encouraging evidence. To quote Smesko, the Dream were “right there” even, as indicated by the final score, the game was played on the Valkyries’ terms and at their tempo. Ideally, Atlanta would prefer to determine the game’s flow and feel. A faster, somewhat chaotic and up-and-down affair would be more favorable. Yet, in a matchup that trended slower and muddier, the Dream led for almost 80 percent of the game. They did not pile up transition points. Nor did they feast on early offensive opportunities. And they barely hit anything from behind the arc. But, they still had the edge for most of the afternoon. That made the loss more painful, but also justifies some positivity. Howard managed to score just 12 points on 14 shots. Reese was silenced after a fantastic first quarter. Jordin Canada’s new-found scoring juice wasn’t there. Back on the bench with Allisha Gray’s return, DeWanna Bonner did not provide a productive injection of veteran experience. Gray herself, with a new-and-improved left hand, looked like the difference maker in the early going, but, after not playing a full game since the first round, lost steam as the game progressed. She still finished as the Dream’s leading scorer, with 19 points on 19 shot attempts. That's her game 🙂‍↕️ pic.twitter.com/QbW4RKxwu5 — Atlanta Dream (@AtlantaDream) October 17, 2026 It’s easy to argue that Atlanta didn’t play well—and, again, almost stole Game 1. They didn’t. And the crux is the clutch. The solidity of Golden State’s identity compared to the shakiness of Atlanta’s was most evident in the fourth quarter. As the final 10 minutes ticked by, the Valkyries, led by Gabby Williams, became more assured and empowered; the Dream experienced an unraveling into indecision and self-inflicted errors. Howard is the easily identifiable culprit. A player who is often more comfortable taking what the defense gives her, Howard attempted to assume the first-option mantle for the Dream down the stretch. Yet, induced into isolation actions by the Golden State defense, Howard’s assertiveness devolved into over dribbling, poor passes and forced drives, unable to to coerce a reaction and rotation from the Valkyrie defense that could, in turn, open up an easy look for herself or a teammate. During the semifinals, Canada was the end-of-game engine for the Dream, with her speed advantage making her a near-automatic paint touch. From there, Canada could zoom to the rim for acrobatic finishes or kick the ball out to a teammate who was ready to take the open shot, or move the ball until such a shot materialized. Golden State, however, was prepared to close off Canada’s attacks, or any other penetration of the paint from Atlanta players. Unless the 3-pointers start falling, does Atlanta have a solution to the halfcourt stagnancy? RHYN3 HOWARD 👌 pic.twitter.com/9TU3mPNR34 — Atlanta Dream (@AtlantaDream) October 17, 2026 Until this playoff run, the Dream rarely had demonstrated poise and precision in the offensive halfcourt. There’s a reason the team has leaned into their defense. They’re a group of elite defenders who are good enough on offense. Howard profiles as a player capable of superstar efforts in the stretch. Yet, she too often settles for contested shots. When she does break the paint, she tends to fade away on midrange attempts or try for a flailing, off-balance finish at the rim, too concerned with evading, rather than embracing, contact. Gray’s game, while effective, lacks on-the-ball diversity; she going to take the 3 or drive. Reese’s halfcourt game is still refining, with her outside shot too inconsistent and drives to the hoop too uncomposed to be a trusted option in late-game situations. Second-chance points, instead, are her greatest value in such circumstances, something Golden State has recognized with the extra attention they are directing towards her when she’s battling on the glass. Canada, as she showed in the semis, might be best suited for the role, except her size becomes an issue against a superior defense. Lessons from a legend 🏆 Jordin Canada reflects on winning two WNBA championships alongside Sue Bird and how those lessons continue to shape her leadership as she chases a third title with Atlanta. #WNBASeason30 | #2026WNBAFinals pic.twitter.com/TtJMHVy3a7 — WNBA (@WNBA) October 18, 2026 Maybe it’s Dream dooming, but the best solution might be avoiding a close game. However, it’s hard to imagine Atlanta escaping in anything resembling blowout fashion, especially in the halls of Ballhalla. This season, the Valkyries lost just five home games, with their worst defeat coming by 11 points. In a seven-game series, Game 2 is not a must-win game for the Dream. Except, it kind of is. In the event of another loss, the Dream can take solace in the series shift to Atlanta, where they will have two home games at State Farm Arena to even the series at 2

item.title: Broncos vs. Seahawks: The No Bull Review
item.description: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Kris Abrams-Draine #31 celebrates with Ja'Quan McMillian #29 of the Denver Broncos after securing an interception during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field at Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a finicky bunch here in Broncos Country. Also, the media is always a fickle bunch of knee-jerk creatures with little to no nuance for this game that we love. Let me lay some No Bull truth down for you all that can hopefully talk some of you back from the ledge into wading into the abyss about Bo Nix and the offensive woes that Fitz-ception and the rest of the talking heads are freaking out about. Credit where it is due The #1 thing that everyone who’s trying to dump on Bo Nix right now is forgetting is that the Seattle Seahawks have an absolutely fierce defense that matches up VERY well against our offense. Their front is one of the best in the game. They schematically crush average run games (and let’s be honest, ours is not average: it is poor). They also make it extremely hard on the back end to complete deep passes. Everyone wants to talk about how bad Nix is, but has absolutely no clue about what happened on the film. I do not have access to All-22, but I can tell you there were NOT people open against that defense. When the broadcast did show us the better angles, our receivers were smothered outside of one singular play. Dial back the perspective a little wider. We just played 6 of the toughest defenses in the NFL, and our two losses came to two of the undefeated teams as it stands today: the 49ers and Chiefs. This game was never going to be pretty offensively. This 6-game stretch was never going to be roses and touchdowns. Perspective is needed Let’s be better fans and think a little deeper. We’ve seen so much of this story before. Bo Nix struggled just as badly last season, the same way early in the season. We looked terrible in a Thursday night game last season. This run game is a stinking hot one and a half-foot-wide cow patty, and our wide receivers are very much overrated and inconsistent. Thinking back a little further, I saw this same story back in the 2015 season. I think a lot of you have forgotten just how pathetic the offense was under Peyton Manning and Brock Osweiler that season. That team got dragged by the defense all the way to the Super Bowl. Take a deep breath, Broncos Country. Uncle Sadaraine is here to tell you this season is not in danger…it is actually just getting started. More on that when we wrap up. For now, let’s dig into reviewing this game. Offense While I love to see a coach dedicated to the run game, I am getting quite uncomfortable with how much we lean into a part of the game that performs so poorly. We ran into 8 and 9-man boxes (loosely…you could say the safety was out of the box, but he was only out by one friggin step) multiple times. I do not understand
item.content:encoded: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Kris Abrams-Draine #31 celebrates with Ja'Quan McMillian #29 of the Denver Broncos after securing an interception during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field at Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a finicky bunch here in Broncos Country. Also, the media is always a fickle bunch of knee-jerk creatures with little to no nuance for this game that we love. Let me lay some No Bull truth down for you all that can hopefully talk some of you back from the ledge into wading into the abyss about Bo Nix and the offensive woes that Fitz-ception and the rest of the talking heads are freaking out about. Credit where it is due The #1 thing that everyone who’s trying to dump on Bo Nix right now is forgetting is that the Seattle Seahawks have an absolutely fierce defense that matches up VERY well against our offense. Their front is one of the best in the game. They schematically crush average run games (and let’s be honest, ours is not average: it is poor). They also make it extremely hard on the back end to complete deep passes. Everyone wants to talk about how bad Nix is, but has absolutely no clue about what happened on the film. I do not have access to All-22, but I can tell you there were NOT people open against that defense. When the broadcast did show us the better angles, our receivers were smothered outside of one singular play. Dial back the perspective a little wider. We just played 6 of the toughest defenses in the NFL, and our two losses came to two of the undefeated teams as it stands today: the 49ers and Chiefs. This game was never going to be pretty offensively. This 6-game stretch was never going to be roses and touchdowns. Perspective is needed Let’s be better fans and think a little deeper. We’ve seen so much of this story before. Bo Nix struggled just as badly last season, the same way early in the season. We looked terrible in a Thursday night game last season. This run game is a stinking hot one and a half-foot-wide cow patty, and our wide receivers are very much overrated and inconsistent. Thinking back a little further, I saw this same story back in the 2015 season. I think a lot of you have forgotten just how pathetic the offense was under Peyton Manning and Brock Osweiler that season. That team got dragged by the defense all the way to the Super Bowl. Take a deep breath, Broncos Country. Uncle Sadaraine is here to tell you this season is not in danger…it is actually just getting started. More on that when we wrap up. For now, let’s dig into reviewing this game. Offense While I love to see a coach dedicated to the run game, I am getting quite uncomfortable with how much we lean into a part of the game that performs so poorly. We ran into 8 and 9-man boxes (loosely…you could say the safety was out of the box, but he was only out by one friggin step) multiple times. I do not understand how this offense wasn’t dialing up a quick slant / out or a play-action audible more often. Either the players aren’t capable of adjusting on the field for whatever strange reason, or Payton doesn’t trust them to execute (or both). But we had many 2 and less yard gains because of running into stacked boxes with a back who looks completely washed and a line that is inconsistent at executing their blocks. Yes, we made 2 drives work with a run game that churned out production. But when that dried up, they just kept hitting the same buttons hoping for it to finally work. It was absolute insanity through the 3rd and 4th quarters. One problem I saw was a problem with design. In the 4th quarter on 3rd and 10, the play design was absolutely mind-boggling to the side Nix was reading. Both outside routes Nix was looking at were in-breaking next to each other with a safety over the top. There was no space for him to find a play to throw to. Just have those guys scissor and give your quarterback a read to throw to one-on-one. They can’t keep a safety over both if you do that. Quarterbacks Bo Nix is not broken. He has regressed this season at some level, but I do expect that at some level when his offseason was spent recovering from a broken ankle and 2nd surgery. I know Broncos Country is absolutely coo coo for Cocoa Puffs when it comes to quarterback play, but you all need to ease up. This is only his 3rd year, and he did NOT have a full offseason to sharpen his skill set. I’m not saying he’s a great quarterback. I think he’s looking average at best. But when we think about how many good defenses he’s been facing, I have to think there’s a really great opportunity in front of him to start rounding into form as the season wears on. I do get frustrated on 3rd down after 3rd down with him not producing something, but I’d love someone to show me all the opportunities he missed because they sure as hell didn’t look to me to be there when we did get coverage angles. Line This line had a good half with really well-executed blocks for two touchdown drives. As the game wore on, they wore down, and the play got choppy up front (especially in the run plays). They ran power a few times that were as good as you will see in the NFL this weekend. I was rather disappointed with Luke Wattenburgh’s bad snap. At what point will he play like a long-term starting center? Running Backs RJ Harvey is the one guy on the offense that is playing inspired football. He’s only getting a couple of handfuls of touches each game, but he’s making them count. He executed a great screen play with a great block from Wattenburg out in space for a 16-yard gain. Later on the same drive, he pulled off another to get the ball inside the 10. He also converted a 3rd and 1 out of shotgun by shooting to the outside. He took a wild cat snap to the house for the 2nd touchdown of the game. He finished with 6 runs for 25 yards (4.2 ypc) and 3 catches on 4 targets for 31 yards. We’re going to go way back with JK Dobbins to spit some No Bull truth this week. JK Dobbins is Lance Ball. He’s a guy we’re feeding who knows the offense but just doesn’t bring anything worthwhile to the table. His touchdown run was a credit to the line (one of their best blocked plays of the game). He had one good run for 16 yards where he actually jump-stepped to avoid a tackle for 16 yards. But he only created 41 yards on 17 carries (2.4 ypc). Without that one 16-yard run, he was 16 for 25, which is 1.57 ypc. This is honestly dog shit production from a running back. The SECOND that Jonah Coleman gets back, he should get a start over Dobbins or Tyler Badie. Dobbins is a detriment to this offense and should be treated as such. He’s supposed to be a power back who can power through tackles, and I just don’t see that in his game this year. Let’s throw in some credit to Tyler Badie for his big conversion on 4th and 3 behind Meinerz and McGlinchey. It was a shame he got injured and was out of the game, as I think he deserves more opportunities given what we’ve seen in front of him so far this season. Receivers None of our receivers are worthy of anything positive this week. They got owned by and large the whole game and did not create separation to give Nix options. Cortland Sutton dropped a pass that hit him in the hands. Jaylen Waddle got dinged up and finished the game, but was only 4 out of 7 targets for 24 yards. The receivers and tight ends were smothered by the Seahawks defense and did not find a way to fight that got them openings. Defense Vance Joseph and this defense deserve all the credit in the world for this win. They were a salient force that does not get enough credit for how well they have been playing. JSN is the Seahawks’ offense. He got his 134 yards on 12 receptions. I will take that all day, and I’m not even kidding. Vance had his guys play a mix of off coverage or press with a safety over the top and set things up so that JSN was never allowed to g

item.title: How to watch Commanders vs 49ers: TV, radio, streaming, injury report
item.description: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 31: Terry McLaurin #17 of the Washington Commanders catches a touchdown against Ambry Thomas #20 of the San Francisco 49ers at FedExField on December 31, 2023 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Washington Commanders are on the road for Week 6 with a bye to follow in Week 7. They are traveling to the west coast to take on the San Francisco 49ers on Monday Night Football. A big game in primetime with a lot of implications for Dan Quinn and others in the organization. The Commanders come into this game with a 1-3-1 record and they made a devastating series of mistakes on the final drive/play of overtime, leading to a tie with the Giants. They need to wipe the stink off that result, but they’ll have a tall task taking on the 5-0 49ers on the road. The Commanders offense will be without RB Bill Croskey-Merritt, but should have their top two WRs who have been dealing with hamstring injuries back. They are also expected to activate CB Trey Amos and RB Jeremy McNichols from injured reserve. Washington will need all hands on deck, and a big game from QB Jayden Daniels to leave California with the win. The 49ers share the best record in football with the Chiefs and Vikings at 5-0. Brock Purdy has been playing at an MVP-level this season, despite the injuries that have decimated the Niners WR room. San Francisco is coming off a hard-fought division win against the Seattle Seahawks. item.title: NBA predictions: Picks for 2027 champion, MVP, Rookie of the Year, and more
item.description: (Photo by Vaughn Ridley/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images It might be harder to predict the NBA right now than it has been at any point in league history. The last eight years have produced eight different champions, and no team has even made back-to-back NBA Finals appearances over that time. The second-apron is breaking up contenders early, and an added emphasis on pace-and-space is leading more injuries that make it so much harder to sustain success year-over-over. The NBA season rarely plays out how we think it’s going to. The New York Knicks weren’t exactly a popular preseason pick to win it all last year, and absolutely no one saw the San Antonio Spurs morphing from a 44-win team to the Western Conference champions. The Indiana Pacers made a darkhorse NBA Finals run in 2025, the Dallas Mavericks did the same in 2024, and Miami Heat got all the way there as an 8-seed in 2023. You might think we can already fast-forward to a Thunder-Spurs rematch in the Western Conference Finals this year, but there tends to be a lot more chaos in this era of the league than ever before. With the 2026-27 season here, let’s make our picks for the 2027 NBA Finals and every major award. For more NBA preview coverage, check my list of breakout player candidates , preseason standouts , and preseason rookie rankings . The Raptors win the Eastern Conference I think it’s fair to frame the East as the Knicks vs. the field. I respect the Knicks, but I’d still take the field in that equation, just because it’s so hard to put together consecutive Finals runs in this era. I was choosing between the Raptors and Celtics for my East pick, and I’m going with Toronto for a few reasons. You usually need a top-5 player to make a Finals run, and Kawhi Leonard looked like that type of player last year. I’m well aware of his constant injury issues late in the season, but hey, Toronto did a good job pacing his body last time he was there in 2019, and I think they can do it again. Scottie Barnes is going to have a monster year as Leonard’s sidekick, and when the two share the floor with sophomore Collin Murray-Boyles , it’s going to be impossible to score on Toronto. Ja’Kobe Walter and Jamal Shead are very good role players for this team, and I think Allen Graves can be a contributor off the bench as a rookie, too.
